newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania sees boost from new IBCA rating.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania sees boost from new IBCA rating.

text.p: Lithuania, trying to throw off the image as a laggard in the race to reform and attract more foreign investment, welcomed on Friday a new BB+ credit rating from IBCA.
But some locel analysts thought the new rating, slightly higher than one awarded by Moody's last year, was too low.
"This rating is too low for Lithuania. The country's macroeconomic figures for 1996 are very good. Inflation is way down and growth is up," a senior financial analyst said.
Nevertheless, "this evaluation will attract more investments at a cheaper price and increase confidence in Lithuania," the office of Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorious said in a statement.
The statement said IBCA originally planned to assign a lower rating of BB, which would have been equal to the Ba2 it was given by New York-based Moody's last September.
That rating was the first one ever assigned to a former Soviet republic. Lithuania regained its independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.
But IBCA changed the rating after Finance Minister Rolandas Matiliauskas provided the agency with more up-to-date economic and financial data.
Inflation was 13.1 percent on a year-on-year basis in 1996, down from 1995's 35.7 percent.
And Vagnorius' new government has pledged to speed reform and privatise more companies.
Vagnorius has forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth this year of five percent. Growth for the first nine months of 1996 was 3.6 percent.
Analysts and government officials said the rating would reduce borrowing costs and increase investor interest.
"This is welcome news...investors look closely at these kinds of things," said Algis Avizienis, the head of the government-run Lithuanian Investment Agency.
"This will certainly cut borrowing costs on international capital markets and that in turn, will push yields down a bit on the domestic T-bill market," said one local analyst.
The Lithuanian government said last week it planned to issue a $200-million Eurobond this spring.
The country made its debut on international capital markets in December 1995 with a $60 million, two-year Eurobond with a 10-percent coupon.
But given modest borrowing needs, few analysts expected Lithuania to bring a large amount of paper before the international markets.
